implementation_notes: Go's concurrency model already makes most shared-memory conflicts disappear: goroutines are isolated by the CSP model, and the idiomatic answer to 'one owner of this state' is a channel with a single owner or a `sync.Mutex` around a small critical section. Adding an STM means introducing lock-free machinery, an implicit read set the compiler does not check, and automatic re-execution - in exchange for removing something Go already made rare. Where a genuine composite update is unavoidable, the honest form is a `select` loop in the owning goroutine: a case that receives an operation, re-checks the precondition against current state, and either applies or replies 'retry', letting the caller loop. That keeps the retry decision explicit and the ownership unambiguous, and it is the same abstract mechanism STM implements (validate-then-act with re-execution), just without pretending to provide snapshot isolation over arbitrary shared memory. If you genuinely want STM in a Go program, the usual reason is that the STM is written in another language and you need an adapter at the boundary - keep it at that boundary rather than spreading it.
alternative: channel with a single owner goroutine plus a select-loop, or sync.Mutex around a short critical section
pitfalls: Sharing mutable maps or slices across goroutines without ownership: Go's race detector will find these, but the STM-shaped fix (a read set the compiler cannot verify) is worse than the bug it fixes.
Using sync.RWMutex and then doing I/O under a read lock, which defeats the point of the reader/writer split.
Retrying inside the owning goroutine rather than in the caller, which blocks every other operation behind the loser.
Assuming 'Go has no data races because of the scheduler' - the race detector exists precisely because that is false.
Importing an STM package for a problem that is really a missing ownership boundary; the channel is the fix.
